lead: A rolling bearing fails by fatigue, not at one fixed load. Heavy load shortens life. Makers give two numbers: C, the basic dynamic load rating, and C₀, the basic static load rating. From C and the equivalent load P you get L₁₀, the life reached by 90 of 100 identical bearings. This chapter computes L₁₀ = (C/P)<sup>p</sup> in million revolutions, then in hours, and handles a load that changes through the day.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.2 for bearing parts, and fatigue from Failure Theories and Fatigue Design.

blocks.text: A ball or roller bearing rarely snaps. It fails by fatigue: after many revolutions a small piece of raceway metal flakes off, called spalling. Life depends on load. Roughly, double the load and a ball bearing lasts one-eighth as long. Standards give two ratings.

items: Basic static load rating C₀, in N: the load that leaves a total permanent deformation of 0.0001 times the rolling-element diameter (ball or roller) at the most heavily loaded contact. Use C₀ for stationary, slow, or heavy shock at rest.
Basic dynamic load rating C, in N: the load at which identical bearings reach a rating life of one million (10⁶) revolutions with 90% healthy. C is capacity, not breaking load.

blocks.text: Both come from the catalogue, not from derivation. For a 25 mm bore deep-groove ball bearing, C is roughly 15 kN and C₀ roughly 8 kN. Use them to form the ratio C/P.
A real bearing carries radial load F<sub>r</sub>, in N, perpendicular to the shaft axis, and axial or thrust load F<sub>a</sub>, in N, along the axis. Fold both into one equivalent dynamic load P.

blocks.where: P in N; F<sub>r</sub> radial load in N; F<sub>a</sub> axial load in N; X radial factor, Y thrust factor, from the catalogue for that bearing.

blocks.text: P is the pure radial load giving the same fatigue as the actual mix. For pure radial load, X = 1, Y = 0, so P = F<sub>r</sub>. For pure thrust load, X = 0, so P = Y F<sub>a</sub>.

Single-row deep-groove ball bearings take small thrust. Catalogue tables compare F<sub>a</sub>/F<sub>r</sub> with threshold e and F<sub>a</sub>/C₀. If F<sub>a</sub>/F<sub>r</sub> ≤ e, X = 1, Y = 0, so P = F<sub>r</sub>. Above e, X = 0.56 and Y comes from the table, typically 1 to 2. Use tables for the chosen bearing type.

sections.h3: Life in revolutions and in hours

blocks.where: L<sub>10</sub> is rating life in million revolutions; C and P are in the same unit (N or kN); p = 3 for ball bearings, p = 10/3 for roller bearings.

blocks.text: The subscript 10 is a probability, not a count. L<sub>10</sub> is the life 90% of a batch reaches; about 10% fail earlier. C = 30 kN, P = 6 kN gives L<sub>10</sub> = (30/6)³ = 125 million revolutions. The same C on a roller bearing gives 5<sup>10/3</sup> ≈ 214 million, because a roller spreads contact over a line.
L<sub>10h</sub> is the life in hours; n is the speed in rpm; 10⁶ turns million revolutions into revolutions and 60 n is the revolutions per hour.
At n = 1500 rpm: L<sub>10h</sub> = 10⁶ × 125/(60 × 1500) = 1389 hours, about 58 days of continuous running. At half speed the hours double.

When the load and speed change in steps, fatigue adds up revolution by revolution. The mean equivalent load P<sub>e</sub> is the steady load that does the same damage: P<sub>e</sub> = [ (P<sub>1</sub><sup>p</sup> n<sub>1</sub> t<sub>1</sub> + P<sub>2</sub><sup>p</sup> n<sub>2</sub> t<sub>2</sub> + …) ÷ (n<sub>1</sub> t<sub>1</sub> + n<sub>2</sub> t<sub>2</sub> + …) ]<sup>1/p</sup>, where P<sub>i</sub> in N is the load in step i, n<sub>i</sub> its speed in rpm and t<sub>i</sub> its share of the time. The bearing then runs at the mean speed n<sub>m</sub> = Σ n<sub>i</sub> t<sub>i</sub>.

For a reliability R other than 90 %, multiply L<sub>10</sub> by the life adjustment factor a<sub>1</sub> of ISO 281: 0.64 for 95 % and 0.25 for 99 %. Some textbooks use the Weibull form L/L<sub>10</sub> = [ln(1/R) ÷ ln(1/0.9)]<sup>1/1.17</sup> instead, which gives 0.54 for 95 %; use the one your data book uses.

figure.caption: Rating life against load for C = 30 kN. At the worked example's 6 kN a ball bearing gives 125 million revolutions and a roller bearing 214; doubling the load to 12 kN cuts the ball bearing to 15.6, one-eighth.

spec.aria: Two falling curves of L10 life against equivalent load from 4 to 12 kilonewtons, for ball and roller bearings, with points at 125, 214 and 15.6 million revolutions.

examples.question: A deep-groove ball bearing on a pump shaft has C = 30 kN. The shaft runs at n = 1500 rpm. The equivalent dynamic load is P = 6 kN. Find L<sub>10</sub> in million revolutions and in hours.
steps: Check units: C = 30 kN and P = 6 kN are both in kN, so C/P is a pure number.
examples.answer: L<sub>10</sub> = 125 million revolutions, which at 1500 rpm is L<sub>10h</sub> ≈ 1389 hours.

examples.question: The same bearing (C = 30 kN) on a conveyor runs 50 % of the time at 3 kN and 1500 rpm, 30 % at 5 kN and 1000 rpm, and 20 % at 8 kN and 500 rpm. Find the mean equivalent load, L<sub>10</sub> and the life in hours.
steps: Weights n<sub>i</sub> t<sub>i</sub>: 1500 × 0.5 = 750, 1000 × 0.3 = 300, 500 × 0.2 = 100. Their sum, the mean speed, is 1150 rpm.
Notice that the 8 kN step, only a fifth of the time and at the lowest speed, gives nearly half of the damage (51 200 of 108 950).
examples.answer: P<sub>e</sub> ≈ 4.56 kN, L<sub>10</sub> ≈ 285 million revolutions and L<sub>10h</sub> ≈ 4130 hours.

traps: Mixing newtons and kilonewtons inside C/P. Convert C and P to the same unit before dividing.
Using p = 3 for a roller bearing. Rollers take p = 10/3, and the same C/P then gives a longer life.
Putting F<sub>r</sub> in place of P when the bearing also carries thrust. If F<sub>a</sub>/F<sub>r</sub> > e, P > F<sub>r</sub> and life drops.
Dropping the 10⁶ when converting L<sub>10</sub> to L<sub>10h</sub>; the answer becomes a million times too small.
Reading L<sub>10</sub> as the life every bearing reaches or as 10% reliability. It is the 90% reliability life.
Using C₀ in the life formula. C₀ guards against permanent denting at rest; only C enters L<sub>10</sub>.

quiz.q: Define the basic dynamic load rating C of a rolling bearing.
quiz.a: C, in N, is the load at which identical bearings reach one million revolutions with 90% still serviceable.

quiz.q: What does the subscript 10 in L<sub>10</sub> stand for?
quiz.a: 10% of bearings fail before L<sub>10</sub>; 90% reach it. L<sub>10</sub> is a 90% reliability life.

quiz.q: Why does L<sub>10</sub> fall sharply when P rises slightly?
quiz.a: L<sub>10</sub> varies as (C/P)<sup>p</sup> with p = 3 or more. A 20 % rise in P cuts life to 1/1.2³ = 0.58 of its old value.

quiz.q: Write the equivalent dynamic load formula and say what X and Y are, and when P equals F<sub>r</sub>.
quiz.a: P = X F<sub>r</sub> + Y F<sub>a</sub>; F<sub>r</sub> is radial load in N, F<sub>a</sub> axial load in N, X radial factor, Y thrust factor, from the catalogue. When F<sub>a</sub>/F<sub>r</sub> ≤ e, X = 1, Y = 0, so P = F<sub>r</sub>.

quiz.q: A deep-groove ball bearing has C = 24 kN and carries P = 4 kN at n = 1000 rpm. Find L<sub>10</sub> in million revolutions and L<sub>10h</sub> in hours.
quiz.a: C/P = 24/4 = 6; p = 3, so L<sub>10</sub> = 6³ = 216 million revolutions. L<sub>10h</sub> = 10⁶ × 216/(60 × 1000) = 3600 hours.

quiz.q: A spherical roller bearing has C = 60 kN and carries P = 12 kN at n = 500 rpm. Find L<sub>10h</sub> in hours.
quiz.a: C/P = 5. For a roller bearing p = 10/3, so L<sub>10</sub> = 5<sup>10/3</sup> = 213.7 million revolutions. L<sub>10h</sub> = 213.7 × 10⁶/(60 × 500) ≈ 7125 hours.

quiz.q: A bearing with C = 30 kN carries P = 6 kN at 1500 rpm, giving L<sub>10</sub> = 125 million revolutions and 1389 hours. The load doubles to P = 12 kN at the same speed. Find the new life and state what this says about overloading.
quiz.a: New C/P = 30/12 = 2.5, so L<sub>10</sub> = 2.5³ = 15.625 million revolutions. L<sub>10h</sub> = 10⁶ × 15.625/90 000 ≈ 174 hours. Life falls to one-eighth; a modest overload can ruin the bearing within days.

quiz.q: In L<sub>10h</sub> = (10⁶/(60 n))(C/P)<sup>p</sup>, why does a bearing last longer in hours at lower speed even though its life in revolutions is unchanged?
quiz.a: Life in revolutions depends only on C/P, not speed. At lower speed those revolutions take more hours; the factor 60n in the denominator makes hours rise as n falls.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plain L₁₀ assumes clean lubricant, normal clearance and good alignment. Life-modification methods multiply it by factors for lubrication, contamination and steel fatigue limit, so catalogues quote longer lives. Condition monitoring uses vibration and temperature to estimate used L₁₀ life and replace a bearing before failure. Search ISO 281, life modification factor and vibration signature analysis.
